name: Therapeutic touch

card.summary: A hands-near-the-body healing practice from nursing that practitioners use for relaxation, pain relief and wound comfort, which people link to calmer, better-rested and better-healing skin and a more relaxed look.
card.aka: TT; non-contact therapeutic touch (NCTT); biofield therapy
card.note: Researchers report no detectable energy field; used as a complement, not a substitute for medical care.

quick.overview:
Therapeutic touch is a practice in which a practitioner holds their hands a few inches above, or lightly on, a clothed person's body and moves them in sweeping passes, aiming to sense and smooth a supposed human energy field. It was created in the early 1970s by nursing professor Dolores Krieger and the Theosophist Dora Kunz.

People interested in appearance come to it through the relaxation chain: calmer nerves, better sleep, less pain and tension, and support for wound healing, which in turn show up in the face and skin. Randomized trials have studied anxiety, pain, sleep and fatigue; the proposed energy field itself has been tested and not detected.
quick.how: A session usually lasts 10 to 20 minutes with the person seated or lying down, clothed. The practitioner centres themselves, passes their hands over the body to assess the field, smooths areas they perceive as disturbed, and then finishes. It is typically offered in hospitals, nursing settings and holistic clinics alongside conventional care, and people who use it for relaxation often report feeling calmer within a single session.
quick.risks: Direct physical harm is rarely reported, since there is usually no contact. The concern raised by clinicians and the American Cancer Society is that it could displace effective treatment for disease; it is described as a complement. Its core claim of a manipulable energy field has not been supported by controlled testing.

lead: Therapeutic touch (TT) is a complementary healing practice in which a practitioner moves their hands near, and sometimes on, a person's body to detect and rebalance what they describe as a human energy field. It was developed in the 1970s by Dolores Krieger, a New York University nursing professor, together with Dora Kunz, a Theosophy figure who served as president of the Theosophical Society in America from 1975 to 1987 [1][16].

In looksmaxxing and wellness circles it is discussed through an indirect chain: relaxation, lower stress, better sleep and less pain lead to a calmer demeanour, healthier-looking skin and better recovery, while practitioners also claim it supports wound healing. Nothing in the practice is a direct cosmetic treatment.

Research on TT is split. Small clinical trials have looked at anxiety, pain, sleep and agitation, and some nursing reviews describe the findings as promising [2][8]. Studies of the underlying claim have not found a detectable field: in a 1998 JAMA experiment, 21 practitioners could not reliably locate a researcher's hand behind a screen [3][16].

chain: Hands passed near the body in a 10-20 minute session
Reported relaxation, less pain and tension, better sleep
Calmer, better-rested appearance and support for recovery
angle.text: People use TT as a relaxation and comfort practice, and the appearance payoff they describe comes from stress reduction and rest rather than from any change to the skin itself. Some practitioners also claim it supports wound healing, which would matter for how scars and skin recover.

paras: TT rests on the idea that people have an energy field that surrounds and interpenetrates the body, and that illness or distress corresponds to imbalance in it. Practitioners say they can feel warmth, tingling or pressure differences with their hands and can then smooth or redirect the field to restore balance [1][16].

Krieger described it as a contemporary form of laying-on-of-hands healing, but said it is unconnected to religion or faith healing [16]. A variant without any touching is called non-contact therapeutic touch (NCTT) [16][7].

The person remains fully clothed, seated or lying down, and a session commonly runs 10 to 20 minutes. The practitioner first centres themselves, then moves their hands a few inches above the body to assess the field, makes smoothing passes over areas of perceived disturbance, and closes the session [1].

Krieger began experiments with Kunz around 1971 and taught the method to her graduate nursing students at NYU, publishing a description in the American Journal of Nursing in 1975 [1]. It spread through nursing workshops and holistic-health networks.

Physicist Alan Sokal reported in 2006 that over 80 colleges and universities in about 70 countries teach it and that about 80 hospitals in North America use it. California's Board of Registered Nursing has accepted TT courses for continuing-education credit [16].

TT is not a cosmetic procedure. Its place in appearance culture comes from three claimed effects: stress and anxiety reduction, better sleep, and support for wound healing. Stress and poor sleep are commonly linked by users to dull skin, tension in the face and fatigue, so interventions that promote relaxation are discussed as supporting the look of the face. Randomized trials have studied TT for sleep quality and fatigue in menopausal women and for labor pain, and earlier trials examined anxiety in hospitalized patients and pain in burn patients [10][11][14][15].

A 1981 trial reported lower anxiety in hospitalized patients after TT [15], a 1986 study examined tension headache pain [13], and a 1998 study looked at pain and anxiety in burn patients [14]. A 1994 randomized crossover design tested non-contact TT with Reiki and other modalities on healing of full-thickness dermal wounds [7].

Nursing-literature reviews describe such studies as suggesting benefit for anxiety, relaxation, pain and wound healing, while noting research is at an early stage [2]. A best-evidence synthesis of biofield therapies assessed the research as a whole [8], and a 2000 systematic review of distant-healing trials examined the evidence for TT among other forms [12]. A scoping review of chemotherapy-induced neuropathy listed therapeutic touch among manipulative therapies that were studied and may be effective options [4]. Recent randomized trials have tested TT against distraction for labor pain and for sleep and fatigue in menopausal women [10][11].

The wound-healing and energy-field claims were also reviewed outside the nursing literature. A 2004 Cochrane review found no robust evidence that TT promotes healing of acute wounds, and was withdrawn in 2016 over concerns about the validity of included studies [16]. Contextual factors such as the therapeutic ritual and practitioner touch are known to drive placebo responses in pain, which researchers cite when interpreting these trials [3].

In 1998, nine-year-old Emily Rosa published a study in JAMA. Twenty-one practitioners put their hands through a screen and tried to say which of Rosa's hands was near theirs. They were correct 44% of the time, within the range expected by chance [9][16]. JAMA editor George Lundberg urged payers to question funding the practice absent experiments showing an effect [16]. The American Cancer Society states that available evidence does not support claims that TT can cure cancer or other diseases [16].

TT is generally reported as safe with few adverse events, because it involves no or minimal contact [1]. The concerns that clinicians and organizations raise are indirect: that people may delay or replace effective treatment, and that resources may go to approaches whose proposed mechanism has not been demonstrated [1][16].

timeline.event: Krieger and Kunz begin early experiments with healing touch [1].
Krieger publishes a description of TT in the American Journal of Nursing [1].
Kunz serves as president of the Theosophical Society in America [16].
Emily Rosa's experiment is published in JAMA [9][16].
A Cochrane review finds no robust evidence for TT in acute wound healing; withdrawn in 2016 [16].
